chapter_summary:
Parallel computers can be classified using Flynn's taxonomy:

1. **SISD (Single Instruction, Single Data):** Traditional sequential processor. One instruction stream operates on one data stream. Example: A single-core CPU.

2. **SIMD (Single Instruction, Multiple Data):** One instruction operates on multiple data elements simultaneously. Example: Vector processors, GPUs, SIMD extensions.

3. **MISD (Multiple Instruction, Single Data):** Multiple instructions operate on the same data. Rare in practice. Example: Some fault-tolerant systems use multiple processors executing the same instruction on the same data for redundancy.

4. **MIMD (Multiple Instruction, Multiple Data):** Multiple processors execute different instructions on different data. This is the dominant class of parallel computers. Example: Multicore processors, multi-socket servers, clusters.

**Shared-memory vs. distributed-memory:**

- **Shared-memory multiprocessors:** All processors share a common physical memory. Each processor can access any memory location. Communication occurs implicitly through shared variables. Examples: Multicore processors, multi-socket servers.
- **Distributed-memory multiprocessors:** Each processor has its own private memory. Communication occurs explicitly through message passing. Examples: Clusters, supercomputers (e.g., Cray, IBM BlueGene).

**Multicore processor organization:**

A modern multicore processor consists of:
- **Cores:** Multiple independent processor cores on a single die. Each core has its own pipeline, register file, and L1 caches.
- **Private caches:** Each core typically has private L1 instruction and data caches.
- **Shared caches:** A larger L2 or L3 cache is shared among multiple cores or all cores.
- **Interconnect:** A bus, ring, or mesh connects the cores, caches, and memory controller.
- **Memory controller:** Manages access to external DRAM.
- **I/O:** PCIe, USB, and other interfaces for external devices.

**Multicore scaling trends:**
- **Core count:** Desktop processors have 4–24 cores. Server processors have 32–96 cores (e.g., AMD EPYC 9654 has 96 cores).
- **Cache size:** L3 caches have grown from 8 MB to 256 MB (e.g., AMD EPYC with V-Cache has 768 MB L3).
- **Memory bandwidth:** Per-core bandwidth has decreased as core counts increase. Memory bandwidth per core is a critical bottleneck.
- **Power:** Power consumption scales with core count. Modern processors use power management (DVFS, clock gating, core parking) to stay within TDP limits.

**Memory bandwidth per core:**

As core counts increase, the memory bandwidth per core decreases. For example, a quad-core processor with dual-channel DDR4 (51.2 GB/s) provides 12.8 GB/s per core. A 64-core processor with 8-channel DDR5 (409.6 GB/s) provides only 6.4 GB/s per core. This is why large multicore systems often use HBM or multiple memory channels to provide sufficient bandwidth.

**Heterogeneous multicore:**

Some processors combine different types of cores:
- **ARM big.LITTLE:** High-performance "big" cores (Cortex-X) and power-efficient "little" cores (Cortex-A) on the same die. The OS schedules demanding tasks on big cores and background tasks on little cores.
- **Intel Alder Lake/Raptor Lake:** Performance-cores (P-cores, based on Golden Cove/Raptor Cove) and Efficient-cores (E-cores, based on Gracemont). The OS uses Intel Thread Director to schedule tasks.

screens.title: Multiprocessor Taxonomy and Organization
screens.subtitle: How parallel machines are classified and how multicore processors are organized and scaled

narration.text: In this lesson we will build a clear mental model of parallel machines and how they are organized on a chip. You will learn Flynn's taxonomy — the four fundamental classes that describe how instructions and data are distributed — and why MIMD dominates modern computing. We'll contrast shared-memory and distributed-memory systems so you can see how communication and program design differ. Then we'll step through the physical organization of a multicore processor: independent cores, private and shared caches, interconnects, and the memory controller. Finally, we'll explore practical scaling trends — what happens as core counts rise, why memory bandwidth per core falls, and how designers respond with more channels, larger caches, or HBM. As you listen, picture a factory: workers are cores, the supply line is memory, and the manager is the scheduler. That factory metaphor will help you reason about trade-offs, and by the end you'll be able to compare architectures, diagnose bandwidth bottlenecks, and explain why heterogeneous cores and power management matter in real designs.

keyIdea.title: Core insight
keyIdea.text: Classify parallel systems using instruction/data streams, and map those classes to memory models and multicore hardware components to reason about performance and bottlenecks.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: Skills you will build in this chapter

narration.text: Over the next screens you will develop four practical capabilities tied to multiprocessor systems. First, you will be able to describe the four classes in Flynn's taxonomy and cite concrete examples for each class. Knowing these categories clarifies why some hardware is best for streaming vector work and other hardware is best for general-purpose multiprocessing. Second, you will understand the difference between shared-memory and distributed-memory machines and the programming implications for communication and synchronization. This helps you choose the right model for an application or debug performance problems. Third, you will explain how multicore processors are organized — what a core contains, how private and shared caches are arranged, and how the interconnect and memory controller are used. That gives you the vocabulary to read datasheets and map performance. Fourth, you will analyze scaling trends: how core counts, cache sizes, and memory bandwidth change with generations, why bandwidth per core often shrinks, and mitigation techniques. Each objective is paired with a milestone so you can verify competency by inspecting hardware specs and computing bandwidth per core.

screens.title: Flynn's Taxonomy — the 2×2 classification
screens.subtitle: How instruction and data streams define parallel architectures

narration.text: Flynn's taxonomy gives us a compact, useful way to think about parallel machines by focusing on two axes: instruction streams and data streams. The taxonomy creates four categories. SISD is the familiar sequential case: one instruction stream operates on one data stream, essentially a single-core C P U running a program. SIMD runs one instruction over many data elements at once — vector processors and many G P U kernels fall here because the same operation applies to multiple data lanes. MISD, where multiple instruction streams act on the same data, is rare; its primary use is in fault-tolerant systems where redundant processors execute different instruction sequences on the same input to detect or mask errors. MIMD is the broad category where multiple processors run different instructions on different data — this includes today’s multicore CPUs, multi-socket servers, and clusters. A common misconception is that SIMD and MIMD are mutually exclusive: in practice a system can contain SIMD units inside a MIMD core. For example, a multicore C P U is MIMD overall, but each core may execute SIMD vector instructions. Remember: taxonomy is a tool to reason about how work maps to hardware and which programming models and synchronization strategies are appropriate.

keyIdea.title: Flynn's taxonomy
keyIdea.text: Classify architectures by instruction and data streams: SISD, SIMD, MISD, MIMD — each implies different programming and hardware trade-offs.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.1 › Flynn's Taxonomy
Definition

Flynn's 2×2 grid

Categorize systems by the number of concurrent instruction streams and data streams.

SISD
Single instruction, single data. Example: single-core CPU.
SIMD
Single instruction across multiple data elements. Example: vector units, GPUs.
MISD
Multiple instructions on same data. Rare; used in fault tolerance.
MIMD
Multiple instructions on multiple data sets. Example: multicore CPUs and clusters.
Analogy & guidance
Analogy: workers in a shop. SISD is one worker doing one task. SIMD is one instruction like an assembly jig that multiple workers use at once. MIMD is a team with different jobs. MISD is like several supervisors checking the same work item; uncommon but useful for safety checks.
Common misconception
SIMD inside a core does not make the whole machine SIMD. Many MIMD machines contain SIMD execution units for data-parallel work.
Key takeaway

Use Flynn's taxonomy to match workload patterns to hardware capabilities and to reason about programming models.

screens.title: SIMD vs MIMD (and SISD vs MISD) — what changes?
screens.subtitle: Execution model, programming implications, and practical examples

narration.text: Let's contrast SIMD and MIMD so you can see when each model is a natural fit and what programming changes they require. SIMD executes a single instruction across many data elements simultaneously. This is efficient for data-parallel tasks like applying the same arithmetic to many array elements. GPUs and vector units are classic SIMD examples. In SIMD you must express parallelism as the same operation on independent data lanes. A common pitfall is trying to force divergent control flow into SIMD; it leads to inefficiency because lanes inactive for some branches still consume resources. MIMD runs multiple instruction streams on distinct data; it fits general-purpose multicore programming where threads follow different control paths. Programming models for MIMD use threads, processes, and message passing or shared-memory synchronization. MISD and SISD are less common: SISD is sequential single-threaded code, MISD is rare and used in redundant or fault-tolerant designs. A useful contrast: SIMD emphasizes data layout and vectorization, while MIMD emphasizes task decomposition, synchronization, and data distribution. When you profile a program, look for sections that vectorize well for SIMD and sections that are inherently MIMD — the best systems often combine both.

keyIdea.title: When to use SIMD vs MIMD
keyIdea.text: Choose SIMD for uniform data-parallel work and MIMD for distinct tasks or control flow; many systems combine both levels of parallelism.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.1 › SIMD vs MIMD
Comparison

SIMD

Single instruction across multiple data lanes; great for vector arithmetic and streaming kernels.

Programming: vectorize loops, avoid divergence.
Example hardware: GPUs, vector units.
Pitfall: divergent branches reduce efficiency.
Comparison

MIMD

Multiple instruction streams on multiple data sets; fits threads, task parallelism, and heterogeneous workloads.

Programming: threads, synchronization, message passing
Example hardware: multicore CPUs, clusters.
Pitfall: synchronization overhead and data distribution complexity.
Concrete example
A matrix multiply can use SIMD inside each core for inner loops while using MIMD across cores to divide rows among threads. Combining levels of parallelism often yields the best throughput.

narration.text: A core design decision for parallel systems is the memory model. In shared-memory multiprocessors all processors can access the same physical memory; communication is implicit through shared variables. This model simplifies programming for many workloads because threads read and write common locations, but it introduces the need for synchronization primitives and careful reasoning about caches and coherence. Shared-memory examples include multicore processors and multi-socket servers. Distributed-memory systems give each processor private memory; processors communicate explicitly through message passing. This model is common in clusters and many supercomputers. With distributed memory you control communication patterns and can scale aggregate bandwidth by adding nodes, but the software must manage data movement explicitly. A common misconception is that shared memory eliminates communication costs; it only hides them — coherence traffic and memory contention remain. In contrast, distributed memory makes communication explicit so it's visible in the code and easier to optimize at scale. When designing or tuning an application, choose shared-memory for tighter coupling and lower latency within a node, and distributed memory for larger scale where explicit control over data movement helps manage bandwidth and locality.

keyIdea.title: Memory model trade-off
keyIdea.text: Shared memory simplifies access but requires coherence and synchronization; distributed memory scales with explicit message passing but shifts complexity to data movement.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.1 › Shared vs Distributed Memory
Definition

Shared-memory

Processors share a common address space. Communication happens through reads and writes to shared variables.

Examples: multicore CPUs, multi-socket servers.
Requires: cache coherence, locks or atomic operations, careful locality management.
Misconception
Shared memory hides communication but does not remove latency or bandwidth limits; coherence traffic can cause contention.

Distributed-memory

Each processor has private memory; data is exchanged with explicit messages, often via MPI or other libraries.

Examples: clusters, some supercomputers.
Requires: explicit communication, careful partitioning of data, and network-aware algorithms.
When to pick which
Use shared-memory for ease inside a node; use distributed-memory to scale across many nodes where you control data movement.

screens.title: Multicore Processor Organization
screens.subtitle: Cores, private caches, shared caches, interconnects, memory controller, and I/O

narration.text: A modern multicore processor is an arranged system of components that together implement parallel execution. Each core is an independent processor with its own pipeline, register file, and typically private L1 instruction and data caches. Private caches reduce latency for frequently accessed data and keep cores from contending for the same lines. Larger, slower shared caches — L2 or L3 — are often shared among a group of cores or all cores to save capacity and improve hit rates for data that moves between threads. The interconnect ties cores, caches, and the memory controller together; common interconnects include buses, rings, and meshes. The memory controller sits between the on-die logic and external DRAM and manages request ordering and channel arbitration. Finally, input and output interfaces like PCIe and USB connect to devices off-chip. A common misconception is that larger shared caches always improve performance; while they can reduce main memory traffic, they also increase latency for some accesses and raise coherence complexity. Understanding these blocks helps you read vendor diagrams and reason about where bottlenecks occur when many cores request memory simultaneously.

keyIdea.title: Processor block view
keyIdea.text: Cores with private L1 caches, shared L2/L3 caches, interconnect, and memory controller form the central hardware anatomy of a multicore processor.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.1 › Multicore Organization
Architecture

Anatomy of a multicore die

Identify the building blocks and their roles so you can reason about latency, capacity, and coherence traffic.
Cores: independent pipelines and registers; run threads.
Private L1 caches: per-core, low-latency storage for instructions and data.
Shared L2/L3: larger capacity caches shared among cores to reduce DRAM traffic.
Interconnect: bus, ring, or mesh connecting cores, caches and memory controller.
Memory controller & I/O: manages DRAM channels and off-chip interfaces like PCIe.
Concrete example
When many cores access the same memory addresses, private L1s can reduce immediate contention, but coherence protocols produce traffic that travels over the interconnect and can saturate links to the memory controller.
Key takeaway

Knowing each block's purpose helps you locate bottlenecks: is the delay in L1 hits, shared cache misses, interconnect congestion, or memory controller queuing?

screens.title: Cache Hierarchy — private L1, shared L2/L3
screens.subtitle: Why levels exist and how private vs shared caches affect performance

narration.text: Caches are organized in levels to balance latency, capacity, and coherence. Private L1 caches live closest to each core and provide the lowest latency for the most frequently accessed instructions and data. L2 or L3 caches are larger and slower; often one L2 is shared between a few cores while L3 may be shared across many or all cores. Private caches reduce contention for hot data, but when threads share data, misses propagate to shared caches and then to main memory. The hierarchy exists because a single large low-latency store is expensive in area and power; layered caches give most accesses a fast path while still providing large effective capacity. A misconception is that shared caches always improve performance: they reduce capacity duplication but can increase access latency for some cores and complicate coherence traffic. An example to clarify: per-core L1 hits avoid interconnect traffic; when L1 misses and data is in a shared L3, the interconnect carries the request but the hit avoids costly DRAM access. Design choices about cache sizes and which levels are private or shared directly shape where your program experiences latency and bandwidth bottlenecks.

keyIdea.title: Cache trade-offs
keyIdea.text: Private L1s give low-latency hits per core; shared higher-level caches increase effective capacity but can raise latency and coherence traffic.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.1 › Cache Hierarchy
Hierarchy

Levels and ownership

Caches trade off latency and capacity. L1: smallest and fastest. L2/L3: larger but slower and often shared.

L1 (private): fastest hits, per-core isolation.
L2/L3 (shared): larger capacity, reduce DRAM traffic, enable data sharing.
Coherence: kept by protocols that generate interconnect traffic.
Scenario
If several threads read the same dataset, a shared L3 can store that dataset once, saving DRAM bandwidth. If threads access private working sets, large private L1s would be ideal but are costly in area and power. Designers compromise with private L1s and one or more shared levels.
Check your understanding
When you see a performance hotspot, ask: is it an L1 miss, a shared cache miss, or a DRAM access? The correct diagnosis guides whether to change data layout, increase local caching, or reduce cross-core sharing.

screens.title: Interconnects and the Memory Controller
screens.subtitle: How on-die networks and controllers shape latency and bandwidth

narration.text: The interconnect and the memory controller are critical for multicore performance because they determine how requests travel and how bandwidth is served. Interconnect topologies vary: simple buses are easy but do not scale, rings reduce contention at modest core counts, and meshes scale better for many cores by providing multiple paths. The interconnect carries cache coherence messages and data between cores and caches; heavy coherence traffic can saturate links and raise latency. The memory controller arbitrates access to DRAM channels and orders requests for efficiency. It also exposes the number of memory channels available, which directly affects total memory bandwidth. A common misconception is that adding cores automatically increases memory throughput; in fact, unless memory channels increase proportionally, more cores only increase aggregate demand, causing per-core bandwidth to drop. Understanding topology and the memory controller's channel count is essential when you evaluate whether a workload is interconnect-bound or memory-bound. For real hardware comparison, knowing whether a chip uses a mesh or a ring and how many memory channels it exposes provides immediate insight into expected scaling behavior. Interconnects and the Memory Controller means the on-die interconnect carries cache and data traffic while the memory controller manages dram channels; together they set the effective bandwidth and latency seen by cores.. In practical terms, how on-die networks and controllers shape latency and bandwidth. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Interconnect + MC role
keyIdea.text: The on-die interconnect carries cache and data traffic while the memory controller manages DRAM channels; together they set the effective bandwidth and latency seen by cores.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.1 › Interconnect & Memory Controller
Architecture

Interconnect topologies

Buses are simple, rings fit moderate core counts, and meshes scale to many cores. Topology influences latency and congestion behavior.
Ring: lower latency for neighboring cores, limited bandwidth for distant traffic.
Mesh: multiple paths, better scalability, hardware routing complexity.
Bus: simple arbitration, poor scaling.

Memory controller

Manages DRAM channels and request ordering. More channels raise total system bandwidth; the per-core share depends on core count.

Concrete question
If two chips have the same core count but one has twice the channels, the second will likely provide higher per-core bandwidth for streaming workloads.

screens.title: Memory Bandwidth per Core — calculation and example
screens.subtitle: How to compute per-core bandwidth and interpret the result

narration.text: Memory bandwidth per core is a practical metric you can compute from a processor's advertised total bandwidth and core count. The calculation is simple: divide total memory bandwidth by the number of cores. This metric highlights why bandwidth often becomes the bottleneck as core counts increase. For example, a quad-core processor with dual-channel DDR4 rated at 51.2 GB/s yields 12.8 GB/s per core by dividing 51.2 by 4. In contrast, a 64-core processor with eight-channel DDR5 and 409.6 GB/s total provides only 6.4 GB/s per core. This drop happens because total memory bandwidth does not scale as fast as core counts. A common mistake is to assume memory bandwidth scales linearly with core counts; DRAM channel increases are limited by package and design constraints. Use per-core bandwidth to decide whether a workload is memory-bound: if your application's streaming requirements exceed the per-core bandwidth, consider alternatives like HBM, more channels, better caching, or offloading work to accelerators. Practically, compute the per-core bandwidth for real chips you analyze so you can make data-driven choices about placement, partitioning, and hardware selection. Memory Bandwidth per Core — calculation and example means per-core bandwidth = total memory bandwidth ÷ core count; use this to detect memory-bound workloads and compare hardware.. In practical terms, how to compute per-core bandwidth and interpret the result. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Per-core bandwidth
keyIdea.text: Per-core bandwidth = total memory bandwidth ÷ core count; use this to detect memory-bound workloads and compare hardware.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.1 › Memory Bandwidth per Core
Calculation

Compute per-core bandwidth

Divide the processor's total memory bandwidth by the number of cores to obtain a simple per-core metric.

/* Example calculations (numbers from the chapter) */ TotalBandwidth_quad = 51.2 // GB/s (dual-channel DDR4) Cores_quad = 4 PerCore_quad = TotalBandwidth_quad / Cores_quad // 12.8 GB/s per core TotalBandwidth_64core = 409.6 // GB/s (8-channel DDR5) Cores_64 = 64 PerCore_64 = TotalBandwidth_64core / Cores_64 // 6.4 GB/s per core
Interpretation

Per-core bandwidth falling with core count explains why streaming workloads may prefer accelerators like GPUs or HBM-equipped chips that provide higher per-lane bandwidth.

Key takeaway
Always compute per-core bandwidth before assuming a many-core CPU will serve a bandwidth-heavy workload efficiently.

screens.title: Multicore Scaling Trends
screens.subtitle: Core count, cache growth, memory bandwidth, and power management

narration.text: Modern multicore scaling follows several observable trends: increasing core counts, growing shared cache sizes, and careful attention to memory bandwidth and power. Desktop chips now span roughly 4 to 24 cores, while server parts reach dozens to nearly a hundred cores — the chapter cites a 96-core example. L3 caches have grown dramatically to hundreds of megabytes in some designs and vendors use techniques like V-Cache to expand effective L3 capacity to very large sizes. Despite these increases, memory bandwidth per core often declines because DRAM channel growth lags core-count growth. Designers use several techniques to mitigate bandwidth shortfalls: add more memory channels, adopt high-bandwidth memory (HBM), increase cache sizes, employ cache compression, and implement aggressive prefetching. Power is another scaling limiter; adding cores increases power consumption, so processors use DVFS, clock gating, and core parking to stay within thermal design power. A common misconception is that cache growth alone solves bandwidth problems; while larger caches reduce DRAM traffic, they cannot eliminate the need for adequate memory channels or faster memory technologies for streaming workloads. Multicore Scaling Trends means core counts and cache sizes have grown, but per-core bandwidth often falls; mitigation involves channels, hbm, caching strategies, and power controls.. In practical terms, core count, cache growth, memory bandwidth, and power management. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Scaling summary
keyIdea.text: Core counts and cache sizes have grown, but per-core bandwidth often falls; mitigation involves channels, HBM, caching strategies, and power controls.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.1 › Scaling Trends
Trends

What grows and what doesn't

Core count: increases across generations (desktop: ~4–24, servers: dozens to ~96 cores).
Cache size: L3 caches have grown from MB to hundreds of MB; vendors use V-Cache to extend capacity.
Memory bandwidth: total bandwidth grows slower than cores, reducing per-core share.
Power: DVFS, clock gating, and core parking are used to control TDP as core counts rise.
Mitigations
Techniques include adding memory channels, using HBM, increasing cache capacity, cache compression, and prefetching. These reduce the impact of limited per-core bandwidth for many workloads.
Quick action
When profiling shows streaming bottlenecks, check channel count and consider HBM or accelerators rather than relying solely on more cores.

screens.title: Heterogeneous Multicore — big.LITTLE and P/E cores
screens.subtitle: Why mix core types and what scheduling must solve

narration.text: Heterogeneous multicore designs place high-performance 'big' cores alongside power-efficient 'little' cores on the same die. ARM's big. LITTLE pairs big and little cores so the OS schedules demanding tasks on big cores and background tasks on little cores. Intel's modern designs use P-cores for performance and E-cores for efficiency with hardware or scheduler assistance to place threads effectively. The advantage is improved energy efficiency: light tasks run on low-power cores while bursts of heavy computation use big cores, saving power relative to an all-big design. But heterogeneity brings challenges. Thread scheduling becomes more complex because the OS must decide which core type best serves each thread, balancing throughput and power. Thread migration costs and cache differences between core types can complicate performance. Cache coherence across dissimilar cores may also behave differently if cache sizes and associativities differ. Modern schedulers like Linux's heuristics and hardware guidance attempt to use performance feedback to make appropriate placements, but optimal scheduling remains nuanced. When evaluating heterogeneous chips, consider both scheduling policies and software behavior: some workloads naturally benefit, others may require tuning to fully utilize mixed cores.

keyIdea.title: Heterogeneity trade-offs
keyIdea.text: Mixing big and little cores improves power efficiency but increases scheduling and coherence complexity that software and OS must manage.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.1 › Heterogeneous Multicore
Definition

Big vs Little cores

Combine high-performance cores with power-efficient cores to run tasks in the right power/performance envelope.
Examples: ARM big.LITTLE, Intel P-cores and E-cores.
Benefit: power efficiency and flexible performance scaling.
Challenge: scheduler complexity and thread migration overhead.
Scheduler impact
OS schedulers use heuristics and hardware feedback to place threads. The goal is to match thread demand to core capability while minimizing costly migrations and cache misses.
Key takeaway
Heterogeneous designs trade scheduling complexity for energy efficiency; measure both power and performance when evaluating such processors.

screens.title: Hands-on activity and assessment idea
screens.subtitle: Inspect a real CPU spec and compute memory and cache metrics

narration.text: This activity turns the chapter's ideas into a practical exercise. Pick a recent multicore processor's specification and extract the number of cores, the L1/L2/L3 cache sizes, the memory channels, and the advertised total memory bandwidth. Calculate two metrics: memory bandwidth per core and cache capacity per core (total shared cache divided by relevant core count). Compare these to a processor from five years earlier to see trends in core count and cache growth. For scheduling and heterogeneity, research the OS scheduler used on that platform and describe how it places tasks on big and little cores or P-cores and E-cores. Finally, write a short conclusion: is this chip likely to be memory-bound for streaming workloads? What mitigation would you suggest? This task tests classification skills, hardware literacy, and simple arithmetic based on vendor numbers. It also prepares you to answer the assessment question: why does per-core bandwidth decrease with core count, and which hardware techniques mitigate that problem? screens.title: Key Concepts — What to Remember
screens.subtitle: Three compact memory and architecture takeaways

narration.text: Let's recap three compact ideas to carry forward. First, Flynn's taxonomy (SISD, SIMD, MISD, MIMD) is a practical tool to match workload structure to hardware. Second, shared-memory systems hide communication but require coherence and synchronization, while distributed-memory systems force explicit data movement and scale differently. Third, multicore hardware is composed of cores with private L1s, larger shared caches, an interconnect, and a memory controller; as core counts increase, per-core memory bandwidth usually falls, so designers compensate with channels, HBM, or larger caches. Keep these concepts in mind when you read datasheets, profile applications, or design systems: classification helps choose programming models, memory models guide communication design, and hardware anatomy points to where bottlenecks will appear. screens.title: What to Remember
screens.subtitle: Three practical reminders to guide analysis and design

narration.text: As a final wrap, remember three practical checks when you analyze a multicore design. First, always classify the workload: is it data-parallel, task-parallel, or mixed? That determines whether SIMD or MIMD approaches are appropriate. Second, measure memory bandwidth per core and compare it to your workload's streaming needs — this simple ratio often explains poor scaling. Third, when hardware is heterogeneous, look for scheduler features and measure migration and cache effects; heterogeneity helps energy efficiency but requires careful software placement. These checks will let you read specs with purpose, pick suitable programming models, and recommend architectural mitigations when you encounter bottlenecks.
